title: The no-arbitrage forward price
objectives: Derive the forward price from the cost of carry.

screens.prose: You will need one share in a year. It costs £100.00 today, and you can borrow at 5% a year. **Plan A:** borrow £100.00 today, buy the share now, and hold it for the year.

state.caption: Plan A costs nothing today and ends with the share

screens.question: How much do you repay on the loan in a year?

hints.text: The lender wants the £100.00 back, and something for the year.
A year at 5% adds $0.05 \times 100$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Repay the £100.00 plus a year's interest at 5%.

byKey.no-interest: You repaid only what you borrowed. The lender charges 5% for the year.
byKey.interest: That is the interest alone. The £100.00 itself is repaid too.
byKey.forward: You took the interest off. Borrowing costs you interest; it does not earn it.

explain.text: You repay $100 \times 1.05 = \text{£}105.00$. So Plan A gets you the share in a year for £105.00, fixed today. Nothing in it depends on where the share price goes.

screens.prose: Plan A fixes today what the share costs you later: the loan repayment. Slide the rate $r$ and the time $T$, and watch that cost.

params.xLabel: Years until you need the share, $T$

derive.caption: Repay {{money(100 * pow(1 + r, P.x))}} at {{fixed(r * 100, 1)}}% when T = {{P.x}}

screens.question: Set the rate to 0%. What does Plan A cost you then?

options.text: £100.00 for every $T$: free borrowing makes holding the share cost nothing
More than £100.00, and more the longer you wait
options.why: You charged for time itself. With $r = 0$ the loan repays exactly what you borrowed.

options.text: Less than £100.00, because money later is worth less
options.why: You discounted the price. Plan A repays a loan, and at 0% the loan repays the same £100.00.

feedback.correct: At $r = 0$ the line is flat at £100.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide the rate to 0% and read the caption at a few times.

explain.text: At 0% the loan repays exactly £100.00 however long you hold the share. Raise the rate and the curve bends upwards, faster for longer times. The cost of holding the share is the interest: its **cost of carry**.

screens.prose: **Plan B:** go long a one-year forward on the share at price $F$. It costs nothing today, and in a year you pay $F$ for the share. Plan A also costs nothing today, and ends with the share and a £105.00 debt.
screens.question: For neither plan to beat the other, what must $F$ be?

hints.text: Both plans cost nothing today and end with one share in a year.
Plan A pays £105.00 in a year for the share; Plan B pays $F$.
If the payments differ, everyone picks the cheaper plan. They match when $F = 105$.

feedback.correct: $F = 105$: both plans pay £105.00 in a year for the share.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what each plan pays in a year.

byKey.spot: You priced the forward at today's share price. Plan A shows that holding the share for a year costs £5.00 of interest.
byKey.interest: That is the interest alone. The forward pays for the whole share.
byKey.discounted: You discounted £100.00 instead of growing it. $F$ is paid in a year, so it carries the interest.

explain.text: Two plans that end in the same place, and cost the same today, must pay the same later. So $F = 105$, the **no-arbitrage forward price**. Any other $F$ lets someone run one plan and the reverse of the other for free money.

screens.prose: A dealer quotes the one-year forward at £108.00, above the £105.00 that Plan A costs. Borrow £100.00, buy the share, and sell it forward to the dealer. Fill in the cash flows.

state.caption: The quote is above Plan A's cost

screens.question: Fill in the missing cash flows, with money paid out as negative.

hints.text: In a year you repay the loan and deliver the share to the dealer.
The loan repays $100 \times 1.05$; the dealer pays £108.00 for the share.

feedback.correct: Nothing today, £3.00 for certain in a year.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add each column, with money paid out as negative.

byKey.r0c2: You repaid only what you borrowed, or forgot the sign. You pay out $100 \times 1.05 = 105$.
byKey.r2c2: Selling forward at £108.00 brings in £108.00 when you deliver the share.
byKey.r3c1: Today you borrow £100.00 and spend it all on the share: the net is £0.00.

explain.text: You put in nothing today and collect £3.00 in a year, whatever the share does. That is an **arbitrage**: borrowing to buy and selling forward is **cash and carry**. Dealers who quote £108.00 get hit until the quote falls to £105.00.

screens.prose: Another dealer quotes the forward at £102.00, below Plan A's £105.00. You can sell a borrowed share today and buy it back later; lesson 12 covers the details.

state.caption: The quote is below Plan A's cost

screens.question: Which trade locks in a profit?

options.text: Buy the forward, sell a borrowed share for £100.00, and lend the £100.00 at 5%
Sell the forward, and buy the share with borrowed cash
options.why: That is the trade for a forward that is too dear. Here you would deliver for £102.00 a share that cost you £105.00.
That is a bet on the share, not an arbitrage. If it ends below £102.00, you lose.

options.text: Buy the share today and hold it
options.why: That is Plan A, which costs £105.00. It does not use the cheap quote at all.

hints.text: The forward is cheap, so you want to be the buyer.
Buying forward gives you a share in a year. Whom could you hand it to?
Sell a borrowed share now and lend the £100.00: it grows to £105.00. Pay £102.00 for the forward's share and return it.

feedback.correct: The lending grows to £105.00; the share costs £102.00; you keep £3.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Buy what is cheap, the forward, and sell what is dear, the share.

byKey.carry: You ran the trade for a forward that is too dear. Here the forward is the cheap side, so you buy it.
byKey.bet: Buying the forward alone is exposed to the share price. An arbitrage needs the offsetting share sale.

explain.text: The borrowed share sells for £100.00, which grows to £105.00 in the bank. The forward delivers a share for £102.00, which you return to its lender. You keep £3.00 whatever the share does: **reverse cash and carry**.

screens.prose: Analysts expect the share, now £100.00, to be worth £112.00 in a year. The rate is still 5%. A colleague prices the one-year forward at £112.00, saying the forward should match the expected price.
screens.question: What is the no-arbitrage one-year forward price?

options.why: You priced the forward at the forecast. Plan A delivers the share for £105.00 whatever anyone forecasts, so that pins the price.
You forgot the financing. Holding the share for a year costs £5.00 of interest.
You grew the forecast by the rate, $112 \times 1.05$. The forecast plays no part.

hints.text: What would you do if the forward were £112.00?
Plan A gets the share in a year for £105.00, with no forecast needed.
At £112.00 you would borrow, buy and sell forward for £7.00 of free money. So $F = 105$.

feedback.correct: £105.00, from the cost of carry alone.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what replicating the forward costs.

byKey.forecast: You priced the forward at the forecast. At £112.00 you could borrow, buy and sell forward for a sure £7.00.

explain.text: At £112.00 you would borrow £100.00, buy the share and sell it forward, locking in £7.00. Everyone would, until the price fell to £105.00. A forecast changes what you think the share will be worth, not what replication costs.

screens.prose: Now in general, with no dividends. Strategy 1: buy the share today for $S_0$. Strategy 2: go long the forward at $F$, and lend $\dfrac{F}{(1 + r)^T}$ today, which grows to $F$ by $T$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: At $T$ both strategies hold one share: in strategy 2 the loan repays $F$, which pays for the forward's share
Equal payoffs at $T$ need equal costs today, or buying one strategy and selling the other is free money
$S_0 = \dfrac{F}{(1 + r)^T}$, the cost today of each strategy
$F = S_0 (1 + r)^T$, multiplying both sides by $(1 + r)^T$

hints.text: Start from what each strategy holds on the delivery date.
The no-arbitrage step turns equal payoffs into equal costs.
Payoffs match, so costs match: $S_0 = F/(1 + r)^T$. Then solve for $F$.

feedback.correct: Same payoff, same cost, then solve for $F$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the payoffs first, then the costs, then rearrange.

byKey.o3: The equation of costs needs the no-arbitrage reason first: equal payoffs at $T$.
byKey.o4: Solving for $F$ comes last, once the costs are set equal.

explain.text: With $S_0 = 100$, $r = 0.05$ and $T = 1$ this gives $F = 105$, your Plan A. With continuous compounding the same argument gives $F = S_0 e^{rT}$, here £105.13. No forecast appears anywhere.

screens.prose: Now the share pays a £2.00 dividend in six months. Whoever holds the share gets it; the forward's buyer does not. In Plan A the dividend arrives while you hold the share. The rate is 5% a year.
screens.question: What is the no-arbitrage one-year forward price now? Give two decimal places.

hints.text: The dividend makes holding the share cheaper. What is it worth today?
Today the dividend is worth $\dfrac{2}{1.05^{0.5}} = 1.95$.
Take that off the share and grow the rest: $(100 - 1.95) \times 1.05 = 102.95$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the dividend's present value off the share price, then grow for a year.

byKey.ignored: You left out the dividend. Holding the share earns £2.00 that the forward's buyer never sees.
byKey.not-grown: You took £2.00 off £105.00. The dividend arrives at six months and earns interest until the year's end: £2.05.
byKey.not-disc: You took the full £2.00 off today's price. It arrives in six months, so today it is worth only £1.95.
byKey.added: You added the dividend. It is income to the holder, so it lowers the cost of carry.

explain.text: The dividend is worth $\tfrac{2}{1.05^{0.5}} = \text{£}1.95$ today, so $F = (100 - 1.95) \times 1.05 = \text{£}102.95$. Check another way: $105 - 2 \times 1.05^{0.5} = 102.95$, the dividend reinvested to the year's end. In general $F = \left(S_0 - PV(\text{income})\right)(1 + r)^T$.

screens.prose: One pound buys 1.2500 US dollars today. A year's deposit earns 4% in pounds and 5% in dollars. A bank sets the one-year forward rate so that the two routes below end with the same value.
screens.question: What is the one-year forward rate, in dollars per pound? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: In a year, £1.04 must swap at the forward rate for the 1.3125 dollars.
The forward rate is dollars per pound: dollars in a year over pounds in a year.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the dollars in a year by the pounds in a year.

byKey.inverted: You swapped the two rates, $1.25 \times 1.04 / 1.05$. The dollar deposit earns more, so a pound buys more dollars forward.
byKey.spot: That is today's rate. The two deposits grow at different rates, so the forward differs.
byKey.dollars: That is the dollars in a year from £1.00. Divide by the £1.04 the pound route gives.

explain.text: £1.00 grows to £1.04, or to 1.3125 dollars. They must swap at the forward rate, so $F = \tfrac{1.3125}{1.04} = 1.2620$ dollars per pound. This is **covered interest parity**: the higher-rate currency, the dollar, is cheaper forward.

screens.prose: An equity index stands at 8,000 points. Borrowing costs 4% a year, and the index's shares pay dividends of 5% a year. Carrying the index for a year costs the interest but earns the dividends.
screens.question: Roughly where is the one-year forward on the index?

hints.text: Is the net cost of carrying the index positive or negative?
It costs 4% and earns 5%: a net carry of −1%.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Net the interest against the dividend yield, then apply it for a year.

byKey.ignored: You charged the interest but left out the dividends. The holder earns 5% back.
byKey.spot: That would need the interest and the dividends to cancel. Here the dividends are larger.
byKey.added: You added the dividends to the interest. Dividends are income to the holder, so they lower the forward.

explain.text: Carrying the index costs 4% and earns 5%, a net carry of −1%. So $F \approx S_0(1 + r - y)^T = 8000 \times 0.99 = 7{,}920$, below today's level. When income beats the interest, the forward sits below spot.

ideas: Borrowing to buy the share now delivers it later for $S_0(1 + r)^T$. Any other forward price is free money.
Too high: borrow, buy and sell forward. Too low: sell a borrowed share, lend the cash and buy forward.
Income from holding (dividends) lowers the forward; costs of holding (storage) raise it. Forecasts play no part.

formula.name: Forward price by cost of carry
formula.note: With no income, $F = S_0(1 + r)^T$, or $S_0 e^{rT}$ with continuous compounding.

summary.trap: The forward price is not the expected future price. It is what replicating the forward costs: the share plus its financing.

quiz.prose: A share costs £50.00. The rate is 4% a year, compounded yearly, and the share pays no dividends.
quiz.question: What is the no-arbitrage two-year forward price?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Grow £50.00 at 4% for two years.

byKey.simple: You used simple interest, $50 \times 1.08$. The loan compounds, so the second year earns interest on the first.
byKey.one-year: That is the one-year forward. The delivery is two years away.
byKey.spot: You forgot the financing. Holding the share for two years costs interest.

explain.text: Borrowing £50.00 for two years at 4% repays $50 \times 1.04^2 = \text{£}54.08$. That is the cost of Plan A, so it is the forward price.

quiz.prose: A forward on a share is quoted above $S_0(1 + r)^T$. The share pays no dividends.
quiz.question: Which trade locks in a profit?

options.text: Borrow, buy the share, and sell the forward
Sell a borrowed share, lend the cash, and buy the forward
options.why: That is the trade for a forward that is too cheap. Here you want to sell the dear forward.
That is a bet that the share falls. Without the share in hand, a rise loses money.

options.text: None: the forward reflects what the market expects
options.why: You priced the forward by expectations. It is pinned by the cost of carry, so a gap is free money.

feedback.correct: Cash and carry: you deliver a share that cost $S_0(1 + r)^T$ for the higher quote.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sell what is dear, the forward, and buy what is cheap, the share.

explain.text: Borrowing to buy the share costs $S_0(1 + r)^T$ at delivery. Selling it forward above that locks in the difference. The share's later price never matters.

quiz.prose: Gold costs £2,000.00 an ounce today. The rate is 5% a year, and storing an ounce for a year costs £10.00, paid at the end of the year. Gold pays no income.
quiz.question: What is the no-arbitrage one-year forward price of an ounce?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the interest and the storage cost of holding gold for a year.

byKey.no-storage: You left out the storage. Holding gold costs £10.00 more, so the forward is higher.
byKey.minus: You treated storage as income. It is a cost of holding, so it raises the forward.
byKey.spot: You forgot the financing and the storage. Holding gold for a year costs both.

explain.text: Plan A borrows £2,000.00, repaying £2,100.00, and pays £10.00 to store the gold. Delivering gold in a year therefore costs £2,110.00. Storage is negative income: it raises the forward.

quiz.prose: A share trades at £80.00. The interest rate is 0%, and the share pays no dividends.
quiz.question: What is the no-arbitrage three-year forward price?

options.why: You charged for time. At 0% borrowing £80.00 for three years repays exactly £80.00.
You discounted the price. A lower forward would need income from holding the share, and there is none.

options.text: It depends on where the share is expected to go
options.why: You priced the forward by a forecast. It is pinned by the cost of carry, which here is zero.

feedback.correct: With nothing to pay and nothing earned, $F = S_0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out what Plan A costs at a 0% rate.

explain.text: $F = 80 \times (1 + 0)^3 = 80$. Carrying the share costs nothing, so the forward equals today's price.
